title: Commercial washers and dryers: motors, drives, bearings, valves and stainless
summary: A coin laundry, hotel or hospital laundry room gives 1–7.5 kW washer motors (often three-phase, with inverter drives), dryer motors and blowers, large bearings, belts, water and gas valves, igniters and stainless drums. Allow 2 hours or more per machine and work in place. They are heavy, run on three-phase and may be gas-fired: lock out the power, shut the gas and drain the water first.

steps.text: Plan to strip each machine where it stands. Washer-extractors weigh 150–500 kg and big dryers 100–300 kg. You are not moving them whole. Clear the floor around the machine, find your way out, and put a second person on every lift (see safety_lifting).

Isolate the power. Coin laundries usually have one isolator or breaker per machine. Switch it off, lock and tag it, then prove it dead at the machine's terminal block: each phase to each other phase, and each to earth (see safety_mains_isolation).
steps.warn: Three-phase supplies can be 400–480 V. Prove your meter on a known live source first and test every pair, not just one.

steps.text: Gas dryers: close the gas valve on the pipe behind each dryer, and the main valve at the meter if you can reach it. Open a window or door. If you smell gas (like rotten eggs), get out without switching anything on or off or making a spark, and let it air for a few hours. Disconnect the gas union only after the valve is shut. Cap the open pipe or fit a plug at once.
steps.warn: A gas leak and a spark can blow up a building. If you smell gas, leave, touch no switches, and ventilate. Keep grinders and flames away from any gas pipe.

steps.text: Water: close the hot and cold inlet valves and open the drain valve or hose on washers to empty the drum and tub into a bucket or floor drain. Pull and cap any chemical supply tubes from soap or bleach pumps.
steps.warn: Bleach, acid sours and alkaline detergents splash. Wear gloves and goggles, and never let two of them mix.

steps.text: Take off the rear and side panels with a socket (8–10 mm bolts are common). The sheet steel is thick and sharp. Photograph the wiring, belts and hoses before anything comes off.

Drives and controllers: a washer's inverter drive holds a charge. Wait at least 10 minutes after isolation, then measure DC volts across its DC bus terminals (often marked + and -) or across the big capacitors. Discharge any reading over 30 V with a resistor lead and measure again (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: A drive's capacitors can hold 300–700 V DC for many minutes after the power is off.

steps.text: Belts: loosen the motor-mount bolts, slide the motor toward the pulley to slacken the belt, and lift the belt off. Photograph the routing and keep the belts.

Support the load before you remove anything under it. Prop a washer's drum and tub on timber blocks before you unhook springs or dampers. A dryer drum sits on support rollers: wedge or sling the drum before you take any roller or drive out.
steps.warn: A washer drum and tub weigh 100–300 kg and the suspension springs are under heavy load. A shifting drum can crush. Never put hands or feet under one.

steps.text: Motors: label the wires at the terminal box with tape (note which lead goes to which terminal), then disconnect them. Support the motor with a block, a jack or a second person, undo the 4 mounting bolts and slide it out. Washer motors weigh 20–50 kg and dryer motors 8–15 kg.
steps.warn: A 1–7.5 kW motor falls hard once its last bolt comes out. Support it before you undo that bolt.

steps.text: Dryers: pull the blower wheel off its shaft by undoing its set screw or bolt. In a gas dryer, unplug the igniter and the flame sensor and undo their screws in the burner box. The dryer's own gas valve comes off its pipe unions only after the shutoff valve upstream is closed; cap the open pipe afterwards. In an electric dryer, unscrew the heating element and the high-limit thermostats from their terminals. Sketch the wiring before you undo it.

Front parts and plumbing: take off the front panel to reach the door-lock solenoids, the coin acceptor and the controller. Unbolt each water inlet valve and pull its hoses and clamps. Unscrew the controller boards, noting the plugs.

Bearings and drums last: drum bearings are heavy and press-fit in a housing. Keep the whole bearing carrier if you can: don't hammer on the bearing. Unbolt or cut stainless panels and the drum. Wear gloves, goggles and ear defenders if you use a grinder.
steps.warn: Cut stainless leaves razor edges and sprays hot sparks. Fold or file the edges.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Washer drive motors.** 1–7.5 kW, mostly three-phase on an inverter drive. A three-phase motor with its drive (variable-frequency drive, or VFD) is a good variable-speed machine drive. Many drives accept single-phase mains and give three-phase out; check the label (see skill_read_nameplate and test_motor).
- **Dryer drum and blower motors.** 0.3–1 kW. Often single-phase with a capacitor, so easier to run from a small generator or inverter.
- **Blower wheels.** Squirrel-cage fans for forced ventilation, forges and dust extraction.
- **Bearings.** Large drum bearings and dryer support rollers are heavy-duty and worth the effort. Press them out carefully or keep the carrier.
- **Belts and pulleys.** Wedge or V-belts and cast pulleys fit mills and pumps.
- **Igniters and flame sensors.** Hot-surface igniters (fragile ceramic parts that glow at mains voltage) and flame sensors from gas dryers. Wrap them for storage. Use them in a gas burner project only with the supply they are rated for and a flame safeguard.
- **Heating elements.** 5–15 kW dryer elements. Only useful where you have a matching supply: a water tank or oven, with a thermostat and an overheat cutoff.
- **Valves and solenoids.** Water and gas valves. Don't re-use gas valves on a different fuel or pressure.
- **Springs and dampers.** Heavy suspension springs.
- **Stainless drums and panels.** A big stainless cylinder: a water tank, a fire drum, a smoker, a compost sieve or a rainwater catch.
- **Hoses.** Inlet hoses and drain pipe.

## Variations

- Soft-mount washers hang the drum on springs and dampers; hard-mount washers are bolted to a concrete floor and have no suspension.
- Steam-heated dryers hold a steam coil and a trap: leave them unless you know the system is cold and depressurised.
- Gas dryers may also have a spark ignition module and a flame rectifier board instead of a hot-surface igniter.
- Old machines may run on 208–240 V single-phase and use belt-driven mechanical timers.

## What to leave

- The concrete or steel bases bolted to the floor.
- Steam and gas piping that is still connected to a live supply.
- Lint filters, hoses and vents full of lint.
